{{short description|American mathematician}}
'''Brian Cabell White''' is an American mathematician who specializes in [[differential geometry]] and [[geometric measure theory]]. He is a professor of mathematics and a former chair of the mathematics department at [[Stanford University]].<ref>{{citation|url=http://mathematics.stanford.edu/people/department-directory/name/brian-white/|title=Brian White|work=Department Directory|publisher=Department of Mathematics, Stanford University|accessdate=2015-11-05}}.</ref>

== Achievements ==
He played a key role in the solution of the [[double bubble conjecture]], that the minimum-area enclosure of two volumes is formed from three spherical patches meeting in a circle and forming [[dihedral angle]]s of 2{{pi}}/3 with each other, by proving that the optimal solution to this problem is necessarily a [[surface of revolution]].<ref>{{citation
 | last = Morgan | first = Frank | authorlink = Frank Morgan (mathematician)
 | editor-last = Hardt | editor-first = Robert
 | contribution = Proof of the double bubble conjecture
 | mr = 2108996
 | pages = 59–77
 | publisher = American Mathematical Society
 | series = Student Mathematical Library
 | title = Six Themes on Variation
 | volume = 26
 | year = 2004}}. Revised version of an article initially appearing in the ''[[American Mathematical Monthly]]'' (2001), {{doi|10.2307/2695380}}, {{MR|1834699}}.</ref>

White graduated from [[Yale University]] in 1977, as the top student in the sciences at Yale.<ref name="gug"/> He earned his Ph.D. from [[Princeton University]] in 1982, with a dissertation on [[minimal surface]]s supervised by [[Frederick J. Almgren, Jr.]]<ref>{{mathgenealogy|id=17380}}</ref> After postdoctoral research at the [[Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences]] of [[New York University]], he became a faculty member at Stanford in 1983.<ref name="gug"/>

== Awards ==
He was awarded a [[Sloan Research Fellowship]] in 1985,<ref>{{citation|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1985/03/10/nyregion/90-scientists-and-economists-win-sloan-research-awards.html|title=90 Scientists and Economists win Sloan Research Awards|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|date=March 10, 1985}}.</ref> and a [[Guggenheim Fellowship]] in 1999.<ref name="gug">{{citation|url=http://news.stanford.edu/news/1999/april21/guggenheim-421.html|title=Three win Guggenheims for past achievement, future promise|journal=Stanford Report|first1=David F.|last1=Salisbury|first2=Diane|last2=Manuel|date=April 21, 1999}}.</ref> He was an [[list of International Congresses of Mathematicians Plenary and Invited Speakers|invited speaker at the International Congress of Mathematicians]] in 2002, speaking in the differential geometry section on the [[curve-shortening flow]] and [[mean curvature flow]].<ref>{{citation|url=http://www.mathunion.org/db/ICM/Speakers/SortedByLastname.php|title=ICM Plenary and Invited Speakers since 1897|publisher=[[International Mathematical Union]]|accessdate=2015-11-05|archive-date=2017-11-24|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171124141541/http://www.mathunion.org/db/ICM/Speakers/SortedByLastname.php|url-status=dead}}.</ref><ref>{{citation
 | last = White | first = Brian
 | arxiv = math/0212407
 | contribution = Evolution of curves and surfaces by mean curvature
 | mr = 1989203
 | pages = 525–538
 | publisher = Higher Ed. Press, Beijing
 | title = Proceedings of the International Congress of Mathematicians, Vol. I (Beijing, 2002)
 | year = 2002| bibcode = 2002math.....12407W
 }}.</ref> In 2012, he was selected as one of the inaugural [[fellow]]s of the [[American Mathematical Society]].<ref>{{citation|url=https://www.ams.org/profession/fellows-list|title=List of Fellows of the American Mathematical Society|accessdate=2015-11-05}}.</ref>
